place-context.text: A model’s visible architecture and proposed vessel use differ from an excavated funerary association. Regional shaft-tomb offerings supply context without identifying this object’s tomb or one shared political authority.

belief.text: The temple model may have covered an incense burner. Its precise function remains an interpretation.

production.text: The small building and platform are made of ceramic; the model represents architecture rather than preserving a full-size building.

name: Colima architectural models
geographicPrecision: Regional locator, not an excavation site.

interval.label: 200 BCE–200 CE
interval.note: Date of the selected temple model; not a lifespan assigned to an entire people.

question: Does a small building have to be a toy?
summary: A ceramic roof, stair and platform make architecture portable. The Met proposes that this model once formed an incense-burner lid. Western Mexican offering traditions and a separately excavated shaft tomb help explain how people connected made objects, funerary places and social relationships, while leaving this model’s precise findspot and use unresolved.

sections.title: Making architecture portable
sections.text: Look at the roof, the space beneath it and the stair rising from the platform. A maker brought these parts together in a ceramic object only 17.8 centimeters high. The miniature emphasizes levels and an approach to the roofed space. It does not give a scale for a full-size building or preserve every wall, material and activity. The catalogue calls it a temple model, but it identifies no particular surviving building, maker or workshop. Describing what the clay represents is a first step toward asking what people did with it.

sections.title: A possible vessel component
sections.text: The museum suggests that the model may have served as an incense-burner lid. If so, architecture was made part of a vessel and its use, rather than a working prototype for builders. This interpretation connects form with an action that the photograph alone cannot recover. No associated burner body or residue result is supplied. Pillsbury compares ancient miniatures with several intentions and functions; a similar building shape need not mean a toy, an identical ritual or contact between the makers of distant objects.

citations.locator: 2015 opening caption; prototype and ritual-vessel discussion

sections.title: Preparing places and gifts
sections.text: In parts of western Mexico, people excavated underground funerary chambers reached by a vertical shaft. Preparing these places involved work on the ground as well as making and arranging offerings. INAH describes vessels, architectural models, stone and shell objects among regional deposits, with differences in chamber form and number. Pillsbury places western Mexican models within this offering tradition and discusses relationships between living people and the dead. Such contexts explain why a small building could carry social significance. They do not establish that this particular model came from a known tomb.

citations.locator: Western Mexican model and offering paragraphs

sections.title: A region of different communities
sections.text: Shared mortuary forms did not make one Colima state. López Mestas describes autonomous villages and small chiefdoms alongside regional differences in ceramic styles. Her account interprets offerings and sculpture as ways of expressing status and relationships with ancestors. These are arguments about social life, rather than direct testimony from every household. Keep the selected model’s own broad date and uncertain history visible when using regional evidence: its architecture starts an inquiry, while excavation and comparison test the explanation.

deeperReading.title: One excavated place supplies an association
deeperReading.text: Huitzilapa, in central Jalisco’s Magdalena basin, offers a different kind of evidence from a regional museum attribution. The excavators’ 1996 abstract describes an unlooted shaft tomb and radiocarbon dates clustering in the first century CE. The 2006 organic-study abstract discusses six interments in two chambers. These associations connect objects and people within a documented place. Only the exposed abstracts were consulted here; the complete excavation record and original dating tables were not read. Huitzilapa is a comparison, not the selected model’s newly discovered origin.

deeperReading.title: Materials reveal work with different levels of certainty
deeperReading.text: The organic-study authors examined burial materials with light and scanning electron microscopy. They report cotton and agave fibres and paper, while many presumed food offerings could be identified only as broad animal or plant categories. Such remains bring clothing, wrapping and the provision of gifts into the explanation. The authors interpret differences as evidence of status. Material identification and social meaning are different steps; neither supplies a complete menu, each participant’s intentions or a universal funerary belief.

deeperReading.title: One model retains two published ranges
deeperReading.text: The current catalogue gives 200 BCE–200 CE. Pillsbury’s 2015 caption gives 200 BCE–300 CE for the same accession. The case keeps the current catalogue range and records the older alternative. These broad dates do not turn the model into an exactly dated witness to the Huitzilapa burial or establish one shared ceremony.

evidenceReading.title: Visible architecture, proposed use and excavated context
evidenceReading.introduction: These source passages are editorial paraphrases. A photograph, a catalogue interpretation and an excavation association support different kinds of explanation.

items.label: The catalogue proposes a use
items.text: The Met describes a roofed structure on a platform and suggests that it may once have been an incense-burner lid.
items.interpretation: Roof and platform can be located in the photograph. The proposed lid function requires interpretation; the supplied views do not establish an associated burner body, residue, exact ritual or excavated tomb. Keep “may” in the explanation.

items.label: An excavated association answers another question
items.text: The Huitzilapa excavators report an unlooted shaft tomb and first-century-CE radiocarbon clustering. The organic-study abstract describes materials around six interments in two chambers.
items.interpretation: This connects evidence with a documented place and burial context. It is stronger contextual evidence than assigning a precise findspot from a style label, but it does not place the selected Colima model there. Full dating tables and excavation figures were not consulted.

items.label: Regional traditions contain variation
items.text: INAH describes different chamber forms and offerings; López Mestas interprets western Mexico through varied styles and autonomous villages or small chiefdoms.
items.interpretation: Repeated practices can connect communities without proving one state, one political border or identical household beliefs. The political account is attributed scholarship, while a particular object still needs its own history.

familyActivity.title: A roof we can see; a use we need to test
steps: Find the roof, a stair and an opening in the supplied photograph. Describe each without adding missing rooms or people.
Open the additional photograph. Find one feature visible in both views, and explain one difference caused by the camera angle.

Ask an adult to read the capsule. Sort these statements: the object has a roof; it may be an incense-burner lid; we know its exact tomb. Which is visible, which is a source interpretation, and which remains unknown?
Make one claim that the supplied evidence supports. Name a further discovery that would help test the lid explanation, without inventing it.
familyActivity.explanation: Source capsule — editorial paraphrase: the Met identifies a ceramic architectural model and suggests a possible incense-burner lid. Western Mexican models occur among funerary offerings, but the consulted record does not supply this model’s precise excavation findspot. The roof is visible, the lid is a proposed use, and an exact tomb is not established. An associated burner body or a securely documented use context could help test the explanation; neither is supplied here. A different camera angle does not represent another ancient period.

review.reviewer: Codex selected source consultation and internal author QA; not independent historian approval
review.scope: Layered object inquiry, regional funerary context, three evidence readings and an answerable image/source-capsule activity. Complete original case interval, identity, claims, object order and prior comparison texts retained. Shared models source preserves the earlier scope and adds a separately identified Colima renewal.
limitations: Huitzilapa papers were consulted at exposed publisher-abstract level, not full excavation/laboratory reports or individual radiocarbon tables. Linked books, original INAH dossiers and the complete Met provenance tab were not read.

Possible lid use, unknown precise findspot, maker and workshop remain distinct from regional shaft-tomb offerings. No single Colima state, universal household belief, reconstructed missing building or contact route inferred. Source-specific chronological conventions and the 2015 caption alternative remain identified.

Both existing local photographs were inspected unchanged; photography date and current remote-image byte parity remain unverified. No source plan or image copied or traced and no new numerical geographic locator accepted. Any draft observation notes require separate modern annotation credit/date/licence before adoption.
Independent historian/community review, real adult/family use, human screen-reader and physical-device/print acceptance remain open.
